questions.stem: Evidence-based practice (EBP) is standardly defined as the integration of a fixed set of core components. How many components does that definition include, and what are they?

options.text: Three components — the best available evidence, clinical expertise, and patient values and preferences
Two components — the best available research evidence and the written unit policy manual
Three components — the clinician's seniority, the unit's tradition, and the equipment already stocked
One component — the findings of the most recently published study on the clinical topic

rationales.whyCorrect: Standard EBP models (Sackett and colleagues; Melnyk and Fineout-Overholt) define EBP as the integration of three components: best available external evidence, the clinician's expertise and assessment findings, and the patient's values, preferences, and circumstances, all applied within a given practice context. Counting the components matters because dropping any one converts the activity into something else: evidence alone becomes uncritical adoption, expertise alone becomes habit, and policy alone becomes compliance. The three-part structure also explains how two patients with the same diagnosis can receive different plans that are both evidence-based.
rationales.eli10: Count them on your fingers: what the studies show, what the clinician knows about this patient, and what the patient wants. Three inputs, and the decision needs all three because each answers a different question. The studies answer 'what works on average,' expertise answers 'does this apply to the person in front of me,' and preferences answer 'is this something the person will actually accept and continue.' Miss any one and you can still make a decision, but it stops being EBP.

questions.stem: A widely cited health services study reported that adults in the United States received about 55% of the care recommended by evidence-based guidelines. What percentage of recommended care was not delivered, and what does this gap say about the purpose of EBP?

options.text: 55% — EBP exists to close the gap between recommended and delivered care, improving outcomes and reducing unwarranted variation
45% — EBP exists chiefly to reduce spending by limiting the number of interventions that may be offered
45% — EBP exists to close the gap between recommended and delivered care, improving outcomes and reducing unwarranted variation
55% — the gap shows that guidelines should be replaced by each clinician's own customary practice

rationales.whyCorrect: If 55% of recommended care was delivered, then 100 − 55 = 45% was not. That shortfall is the practical argument for EBP: its purpose is to move what is already known from the literature into everyday decisions so patients reliably receive care most likely to help them, and so that differences in care reflect patient need rather than local habit (unwarranted variation). Cost savings may follow when ineffective care is dropped, but cost control is a by-product, not the aim, and the gap is evidence that guidelines are underused rather than evidence that they are wrong.

questions.stem: A new nurse asks why a certain dressing is changed every 8 hours and is told, "That is how it has always been done here." Of the three components of an EBP decision, how many does this justification supply, and what should the nurse do?

Two components — long-standing routine reflects both clinical expertise and patient preference
One component — an established unit routine counts as the clinical expertise component
Three components — a practice that has persisted this long has already been shown to be evidence-based

Expertise means judgment built from assessing patients and reasoning about their responses; a schedule inherited from whoever set it up years ago carries none of that. Six projects — research applies published findings at the bedside, whereas EBP generates new knowledge
Six projects — research generates new knowledge, whereas EBP applies existing best evidence to clinical decisions

2042 — the delay illustrates that most published findings are eventually overturned

questions.stem: After a unit implements an evidence-based fall-prevention bundle, its fall rate goes from 8 falls per 1000 patient-days to 5 falls per 1000 patient-days. During the outcome-evaluation step of the EBP process, how should the team describe this result?

A 62.5% relative reduction, which means falls on the unit were very nearly eliminated

questions.stem: Which statement best defines the null hypothesis in a quantitative nursing study?

questions.stem: Which characteristic is required for a hypothesis to be usable in a research study?

options.text: It must take a defensible ethical position about the practice being studied
It must be worded so that the study's results will confirm what the researcher expects

questions.stem: A hypothetical education study crosses 2 teaching formats (video, in-person) with 3 session lengths (10, 20, and 30 minutes), and every possible combination is used. How many distinct study groups does this design create?

rationales.whyCorrect: When two independent variables are fully crossed, the number of groups equals the product of their levels, so 2 times 3 equals 6 combinations. Adding the levels (2 plus 3 equals 5) is the common error and would describe a design in which the two variables were never combined at all. Counting cells correctly matters because each combination must be scheduled, staffed, assigned, and analyzed as its own condition.

A crossed study design is literally that grid: each square is a real group of participants receiving one specific combination, which is why you multiply the numbers of levels instead of adding them.

questions.stem: A researcher enrolls 120 volunteers and places them evenly into two study groups: one group receives a new relaxation program and the other receives the usual study-skills session. Which statement best describes the defining feature of an experimental study design?

options.text: The researcher records outcomes as they occur without altering participants' routines.
The researcher controls who receives the intervention by assigning participants to conditions.
The researcher sorts participants by an outcome they already have and traces their history.
The researcher measures the exposure and the outcome at one time point in one sample.

rationales.whyCorrect: An experimental design is defined by researcher manipulation of the independent variable: the investigator, not the participant or circumstance, determines who receives the intervention and who receives the comparison condition. Options A, C, and D describe observational approaches (naturalistic follow-up, case-control, and cross-sectional), in which the researcher only measures exposures that already exist. Because the investigator controls assignment, experimental designs are the strongest single-study basis for causal claims about an intervention.
rationales.eli10: Two ways to study whether a plant food helps tomatoes grow. First: walk the neighborhood, write down whose plants already got plant food, and measure heights. Second: hand out plant food yourself, so these ten pots get it and those ten do not. Only the second is an experiment, because you decided who got treated. When you make that decision, the two groups differ mainly in the one thing you handed out; when the world decides, they may differ in a dozen ways you never recorded.

Options A, C, and D describe observational approaches (naturalistic follow-up, case-control, and cross-sectional), in which the researcher only measures exposures that already exist. questions.stem: Investigators enroll 800 nurses, collect dietary information in 4 waves spaced 2 years apart, and record who develops hypertension over the full follow-up period. Which feature makes this an observational study rather than an experimental one?

options.text: The investigators gather data on several occasions instead of only once at baseline.
The investigators follow participants forward in time rather than backward in time.
The investigators measure diet as participants already eat it instead of assigning a diet.
The investigators recruit a large sample instead of a small convenience sample.

rationales.whyCorrect: Observational research is defined by the absence of researcher-controlled assignment: exposures such as diet are recorded as they naturally occur, which is exactly what option C describes. The distinction matters because an unassigned exposure leaves open the possibility that people who eat differently also differ in other ways that affect blood pressure.

questions.stem: What is the primary purpose of random assignment in a trial that randomizes 200 participants in a 1:1 ratio to an intervention group or a control group?

options.text: To distribute participant characteristics across the groups by chance so the groups begin comparable
To ensure that the enrolled sample mirrors the demographics of the wider population
To keep participants and data collectors unaware of which condition each person received
To make certain that an identical number of participants completes each group's protocol

rationales.whyCorrect: Random assignment allocates participants to conditions by chance, so measured and unmeasured characteristics tend to be spread evenly between groups at baseline. Because the groups start out similar, a later difference in outcomes can more credibly be attributed to the intervention. Option B describes random selection, which concerns how the sample is drawn from a population rather than how it is split; option C describes blinding; and option D describes retention, which randomization does not control once the trial is under way.

Note what it does not do: it splits the people you already enrolled, so it cannot make an unrepresentative sample representative, and it cannot stop people from dropping out later.

questions.stem: A cohort study enrolls exposed and unexposed workers in 2020 and follows them for 5 years, while a case-control study of the same research question is run separately. Which comparison of the two designs is accurate?

options.text: The cohort starts with exposure and follows forward to outcomes; the case-control starts with outcomes.
The cohort study assigns the 2020 exposure to the workers, whereas the case-control study only records it.
Both designs start with the outcome and trace exposures backward through existing employment records.
Only the case-control design is observational; the cohort's 5-year follow-up makes it a true experiment.

questions.stem: A researcher delivers a new hand-hygiene training program to all 45 staff members at Clinic A and compares infection rates with the 55 untrained staff members at Clinic B, for a combined total of 100 staff. Which classification best fits this study?

options.text: True experimental, because two groups are compared and one of them receives an intervention
Quasi-experimental, because an intervention is delivered but participants are not randomly assigned
Observational cohort, because the researcher only compared two groups that already existed
Cross-sectional, because both clinics are examined during the same overall time period

rationales.whyCorrect: Quasi-experimental designs include researcher manipulation of the independent variable but lack random assignment to conditions; here, group membership is fixed by clinic site. rationales.eli10: There are two things a researcher can control: whether an intervention is delivered, and how people land in the groups. A true experiment controls both. questions.stem: A team plans a trial with 60 participants in the intervention group and an equal number in the comparison group, 120 in all. What would most likely be lost if they instead studied the intervention group alone?

options.text: The intervention could no longer be delivered to participants in a standardized way.
Participants could no longer be measured both before and after the program.
The study would automatically be reclassified as a case-control investigation.
There would be no basis for estimating what would have happened without the intervention.

Subtract their change from the treated group's change and what remains is attributable to the intervention. With one group there is nothing to subtract.

questions.stem: Which example describes an experimental study of fatigue in a sample of 90 people divided evenly among 3 study arms?

questions.stem: A team wants to know whether decades-long exposure to an industrial solvent raises cancer risk; workers are first assessed at age 20 and followed for 40 years. Why is an observational design appropriate for this question?

options.text: Deliberately assigning people to a suspected harmful exposure is unethical, so it can only be observed.
Observational designs let the researcher control the dose and duration of the exposure studied.
Observational designs eliminate the influence of participant characteristics on the outcome.
Observational designs generally provide stronger evidence of causation than experiments provide.

rationales.whyCorrect: An experiment requires the researcher to assign the exposure, which is ethically unacceptable when the exposure is suspected of causing harm; a 40-year latency adds a practical barrier as well. What remains is to study people whose jobs already exposed them and compare their outcomes with similar unexposed workers. The trade-off is honest: nobody was put at risk by the study, but because the researcher did not control exposure, other differences between exposed and unexposed workers must be accounted for.

questions.stem: An experimental trial on a research question enrolls 250 participants, while an observational study of the same question enrolls 12,500 participants. Which comparison of the two designs is accurate?

options.text: The observational study supports causal conclusions more directly because it enrolled far more participants.

questions.stem: Investigators have been recording outcomes at 6 clinics, some of which adopted a new discharge-teaching method on their own. Which change would convert this into a true experimental study, with 3 clinics per condition?

options.text: Increasing the number of clinics observed and extending the length of the follow-up period

Having the investigators randomly assign the 6 clinics, 3 to the new method and 3 to the usual method

rationales.whyCorrect: A true experiment requires the investigator to both manipulate the independent variable and allocate units to conditions at random; assigning clinics to the new or usual method accomplishes both, here at the cluster level rather than the individual level. Only investigator assignment changes the design category.

Watching longer, watching more sites, or adjusting for age afterward cannot undo who chose what, because adjustment only fixes differences you thought to measure. Drawing 3 clinic names for the new method replaces self-selection with chance, and that single move is what makes the design experimental.

questions.stem: During data collection, a research scale is checked against a certified 50 kg calibration weight and displays 51 kg on all ten checks. Because the error is the same size and in the same direction every time, it is systematic error (bias) rather than random error. What is the size of the systematic error, in kilograms?

rationales.whyCorrect: The observed value minus the true value is 51 - 50 = 1 kg, and that same offset repeats on every measurement. Systematic error shifts every observation in one direction, so it distorts the sample mean and is a form of instrumentation (measurement) bias; random error, by contrast, scatters in both directions and largely averages out as n grows. Because the offset is constant, enlarging the sample will not remove it - only recalibrating the instrument or applying a correction factor will. Note that 0.02 is the relative error (1/50), a proportion rather than a quantity in kilograms.
rationales.eli10: Picture a ruler whose first inch was snapped off, so it starts at the 1-inch mark instead of 0. Every object you measure comes out exactly 1 inch too long - not sometimes long and sometimes short, but always long by the same amount. Measuring a hundred more objects will not cancel that out, because the mistake never changes direction. An error that always leans the same way is systematic error, and the only fix is repairing the instrument, not collecting more data.

questions.stem: A trial of a fall-prevention program enrolls 300 residents at a single retirement community; 285 of them are women and the average age is 82. The study is well randomized and carefully controlled, so internal validity is strong, but the makeup of the sample limits external validity (generalizability). What percentage of the enrolled sample is female?

rationales.whyCorrect: 285 / 300 x 100 = 95%, leaving only 5% (15 residents) male. Internal validity concerns whether the study's own design supports a causal conclusion about its participants; external validity concerns whether that conclusion transfers to other people, settings, or times. A nearly all-female sample of very old adults from one facility can support a strong internal conclusion while still giving weak grounds for applying the program to men or to community-dwelling older adults. The two properties are independent: tightening eligibility criteria often improves internal validity while narrowing external validity.

questions.stem: A questionnaire about workplace stress is mailed to 500 nurses, and 150 usable surveys are returned. Nonresponse bias becomes a concern when the people who do not answer differ systematically from the people who do. What is the nonresponse rate for this survey?

The number itself is not the bias; the bias arises when nonresponders differ from responders on the variable being measured. Here the most overworked nurses may be exactly the ones with no time to reply, so measured stress would be pulled downward. Nonresponse bias is a species of selection bias, and researchers probe it by comparing responders and nonresponders on available characteristics or by intensively following up a random subsample of nonresponders.

questions.stem: In an observational study, the crude risk ratio linking a dietary supplement to respiratory infection is 2.4. After adjusting for participants' baseline exercise habits, the risk ratio falls to 1.2. The change-in-estimate approach quantifies confounding as percent change = (crude - adjusted) / adjusted x 100, reported as an absolute value. What is the magnitude of confounding by exercise habits?

rationales.whyCorrect: Substituting gives (2.4 - 1.2) / 1.2 x 100 = 100%, far above the roughly 10% shift epidemiologists treat as evidence that a variable is acting as a confounder. Exercise qualifies because it independently predicts infection and is unevenly distributed across supplement users, without lying on the causal pathway between supplement and infection. Here the confounder inflated the apparent association away from the null, so the crude figure overstated the supplement's link to infection. Confounding is addressed by design (randomization, restriction, matching) or by analysis (stratification, multivariable adjustment). Dividing by the crude value instead of the adjusted value yields the incorrect 50%.

Little exercise on its own raises infection risk, so the supplement group got sick more often for a reason that had nothing to do with the supplement. Comparing only people with similar exercise habits strips that reason out, and the apparent effect collapses from 2.4 to 1.2. When an estimate moves that much after adjustment, the variable you adjusted for was carrying part of the story all along.

questions.stem: A 12-week trial enrolls 240 participants in the intervention group and 240 in the control group. By week 12, 36 participants have withdrawn from the intervention group and 12 from the control group. Differential attrition threatens internal validity because the remaining groups may no longer be comparable. How many percentage points higher is attrition in the intervention group?

rationales.whyCorrect: Attrition is 36/240 = 15% in the intervention group and 12/240 = 5% in the control group, a difference of 10 percentage points. What converts ordinary sample loss into attrition bias is that dropout is unequal and plausibly caused by the intervention itself - side effects, time burden, or lack of perceived benefit - so the balance randomization created at baseline is undone by week 12. questions.stem: Two raters independently classify 100 charts into two categories, and each rater assigns about half the charts to each category. questions.stem: A unit logs the number of patient falls in each of eight months, recorded in calendar order: 4, 2, 9, 2, 3, 8, 5, 7. Which pair of values correctly reports the median and the mode?

questions.stem: In a study, clinical group A contains 10 students with a mean skills score of 80, and group B contains 30 students with a mean of 90. What is the mean score for all 40 students combined?

rationales.whyCorrect: A combined mean must be weighted by group size, because each group contributes its own total rather than its own average: (10 x 80 + 30 x 90) / 40 = 3500 / 40 = 87.5. Option B (85) is the common error of averaging the two means as though the groups were equal in size, option A (82.5) reverses the weights, and option C (90) ignores group A entirely. Because group B is three times larger, the combined mean sits much closer to 90 than to 80.

questions.stem: A pre-nursing research class records resting pulse rates for 200 healthy adults. The mean is 72 beats/min with a standard deviation of 6 beats/min. Which statement best describes what the standard deviation of 6 tells the class?

options.text: Half of the recorded pulse rates lie 6 beats/min above the mean and half lie 6 beats/min below it.
The highest and the lowest recorded pulse rates differ from each other by 6 beats/min.
Six percent of the recorded pulse rates fall outside of the expected clinical range.
Individual pulse rates typically differ from the mean by about 6 beats/min in either direction.

questions.stem: In a data set that follows a normal distribution, approximately what percentage of values falls within one standard deviation on either side of the mean?

rationales.whyCorrect: The empirical rule (68-95-99.7 rule) for a normal distribution states that about 34 percent of values lie between the mean and one SD above it, and another 34 percent lie between the mean and one SD below it, totaling about 68 percent. Roughly 95 percent fall within two SDs and about 99.7 percent within three. Fifty percent describes the proportion below the mean in any symmetric distribution, not the plus-or-minus one SD band.
rationales.eli10: A normal curve is tallest at the mean and thins out toward both edges, so most observations sit close to the center. Push the boundaries out to two standard deviations and you capture about 95 out of 100; three standard deviations captures about 99.7. questions.stem: A statistics handout reports that a set of student scores has a variance of 81. Which statement correctly describes the relationship between variance and standard deviation for these scores?

options.text: The standard deviation is the variance divided by two, so the standard deviation is 40.5.
The standard deviation is the square root of the variance, so the standard deviation is 9.
The variance is the square root of the standard deviation, so the standard deviation is 6561.
The standard deviation equals the variance, so it is 81 reported in squared score units.

rationales.whyCorrect: Variance is the average of the squared deviations from the mean, so its units are the squared units of the original measurement and are hard to interpret directly. This is why published research reports mean plus or minus SD rather than mean plus or minus variance.

The square root reverses both problems at once: the square root of 81 is 9, and 9 is back on the same scale as the scores. Variance and standard deviation carry identical information about spread, but only the standard deviation can be added to or subtracted from the mean.

questions.stem: An instructor adds 5 bonus points to every student's exam score. One student had 80 and another had 76. What happens to the standard deviation of the class scores?

options.text: It decreases, because the higher scores now cluster closer to the maximum score.
It increases by 5 points, because every score in the class moved 5 points higher.
It stays the same, because every score's distance from the mean is unchanged.
It is multiplied by 5, because the same constant was applied to every score.

Multiplying every score by a constant is different; that would scale the standard deviation by the same factor.

Contrast this with doubling every score, which would stretch the gaps and double the standard deviation.

questions.stem: Two nursing units each report a mean patient satisfaction score of 80. Unit A has a standard deviation of 3 and Unit B has a standard deviation of 9. Which comparison is accurate?

options.text: Unit B's scores are spread about three times as widely around the mean as Unit A's scores are.

questions.stem: A set of exam scores runs from a low of 52 to a high of 98, giving a range of 46 points. What is the primary advantage of reporting the standard deviation rather than relying on that range?

options.text: The standard deviation incorporates every value's distance from the mean, not just the two extreme scores.
The standard deviation converts the raw scores into percentages, which are easier to compare across tests.
The standard deviation reports spread in squared units, which is more precise than the raw units of the range.
The standard deviation reveals whether the distribution of scores is symmetric or skewed.

rationales.whyCorrect: The range uses only the maximum and minimum, so it is determined by two observations and shifts dramatically if a single outlier enters the data. It reports spread in the original units (variance is the squared-unit measure), does not convert scores to percentages, and does not by itself identify the shape of the distribution.
rationales.eli10: Judging spread by the range is like describing a class by interviewing only the tallest and shortest student. Add one unusually tall newcomer and the answer jumps from 46 to something much larger, even though nobody else changed. Standard deviation asks every observation how far it sits from the mean and combines all of those answers, so a single unusual value moves it only a little. More information goes in, and a more stable number comes out.

questions.stem: Hospital length-of-stay values in a sample have a mean of 62 hours and a median of 55 hours, with a long tail of unusually long stays. Which statement accurately describes this distribution relative to a normal distribution?

options.text: The distribution is symmetric, so the 68-95-99.7 rule applies to these data with full precision.
The tail extends toward the lower values, which is what pulls the mean below the median.
The tail extends toward the higher values, so the empirical rule does not describe these data accurately.
The long tail lowers the standard deviation, so mean plus or minus SD understates the true spread.

questions.stem: Scores on a hypothetical screening questionnaire are normally distributed with a mean of 100 and a standard deviation of 15. A participant scores 130. Which statement correctly reports the z-score and its meaning?

questions.stem: A student computes the standard deviation of five practice quiz scores: 15, 15, 20, 25, and 25 points. Choice D is the variance, choice C skips the division entirely, and choice A results from dividing by n instead of n minus 1.

Divide by n minus 1, which is 4, not 5, because using the sample's own mean uses up one piece of information; that gives a variance of 25. Take the square root and the standard deviation is 5 points, back in the same units as the quiz scores. Stopping at 25 reports the variance, a common error.

questions.stem: A study reports a sample of 100 observations with a standard deviation of 20 units. Which statement accurately compares the standard deviation with the standard error of the mean for this sample?

options.text: Both values equal 20 units, because the standard error is just another name for the spread of the observed data.
The standard error is 20 units and the SD is 2 units, because SD equals the standard error divided by the root of n.
The standard error is 200 units, because it multiplies the standard deviation by the square root of the 100 observations.
The 20-unit standard deviation describes individual spread; the 2-unit standard error describes spread of sample means.

rationales.whyCorrect: Standard deviation quantifies variability among individual observations, whereas the standard error of the mean quantifies how much a sample mean would vary across repeated samples; it equals SD divided by the square root of n, so 20 divided by the square root of 100 equals 2. Treating the two as interchangeable makes reported results look far more precise than the data support.

Averages are steadier than individuals because one extreme person gets diluted by the other 99, and that steadying effect is exactly the square root of n. questions.stem: A screening test is administered to 100 people who are already known (by a gold-standard reference test) to have a particular condition. Ninety of them test positive. Which term and value correctly describe this result?

It is calculated only within the diseased group, so it says nothing about disease-free people (that is specificity) and nothing about how likely a positive result is to be correct in a given population (that is positive predictive value, which also requires knowing how many disease-free people tested positive). Sensitivity is the property clinicians rely on when the goal is to avoid missing cases.

Nobody healthy was tested here, which is why this number cannot be specificity or a predictive value; those need information about disease-free people or about the full set of positive results.

questions.stem: In a hypothetical cohort, 400 healthy volunteers are followed for one year and 100 of them develop the outcome of interest. Which term and value best describe the quantity 100/400?

Relative risk and absolute risk reduction both require a second group for comparison, and only one group exists here. Absolute risk is the baseline probability from which all comparative risk measures are built.

Level IV, evidence from well-designed case-control or cohort studies
Level III, evidence from a controlled trial without randomization

rationales.whyCorrect: The investigators introduced an intervention and included a concurrent comparison group, so this is a controlled trial; because assignment was made by convenience rather than by chance, it is quasi-experimental, which the seven-level system places at Level III. It is not Level II, since no randomization occurred, and not Level I, since no synthesis of trials was performed. It is also not Level IV: case-control and cohort designs observe exposures that patients or clinicians already have, whereas here the investigators assigned and delivered the protocol themselves.
rationales.eli10: Two features determine the rung. First, is there a concurrent comparison group? Yes, the second unit. Second, was assignment made by chance? No, a manager decided. A study that manipulates an intervention earns experimental standing, and randomization earns the top experimental rung; giving up the coin flip costs exactly one step, landing at Level III. The manager's choice is the whole problem: units are rarely chosen at random, so the unit selected may already have had better staffing or a different patient mix.

It is not Level II, since no randomization occurred, and not Level I, since no synthesis of trials was performed. It is also not Level IV: case-control and cohort designs observe exposures that patients or clinicians already have, whereas here the investigators assigned and delivered the protocol themselves.

questions.stem: Under the GRADE approach, a body of evidence made up of randomized trials begins at high certainty, scored 4. Reviewers then downgrade one level for serious risk of bias and one level for serious imprecision. What is the resulting certainty rating?

options.text: High certainty, rated 4, because randomized designs keep the rating they start with
Moderate certainty, rated 3, because a body of randomized trials may be downgraded only once
Low certainty, rated 2, because each serious limitation lowers the rating by one level
Very low certainty, rated 1, because any risk of bias drops evidence to the lowest rating

rationales.whyCorrect: GRADE rates certainty on four levels, high, moderate, low, and very low, with bodies of randomized evidence starting at high. Each serious concern across the domains of risk of bias, imprecision, inconsistency, indirectness, and publication bias lowers the rating by one level, so 4 minus 2 equals 2, which is low certainty. There is no cap of a single downgrade, and no single domain automatically drives evidence to the floor. The item illustrates the central GRADE principle that design sets the starting point while conduct and results determine where the evidence finally lands.
rationales.eli10: GRADE keeps two judgments apart: what kind of study produced the evidence, and how well that study was actually carried out. The design sets your opening score, so randomized trials open at 4. Then reviewers audit the work domain by domain, and each serious problem they verify costs one step, cumulatively. Two verified problems leaves 2, labeled low certainty. The practical lesson is that 'it was a randomized trial' is a starting claim, not a finishing one, and a poorly conducted randomized body of evidence can end up rated no better than a well-conducted observational one.

questions.stem: A meta-analysis of six randomized trials reports a pooled mean difference in mobility score of 0.6 points, 95% CI -0.2 to 1.4. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: The 1.6-point-wide interval includes 0, so the pooled result is not statistically significant
The 1.6-point-wide interval dips below 0, showing that the intervention worsens mobility
The 0.6-point pooled gain is significant because a meta-analysis of trials is Level I evidence
The findings should be discarded because an interval this wide proves the six trials disagreed

rationales.whyCorrect: The interval runs from -0.2 to 1.4, a width of 1.6 points, and because it contains 0 the data remain compatible with no difference at all, so the pooled effect is not statistically significant at the 0.05 level. The level of evidence describes the design used to answer the question, not the direction or strength of the answer, so a Level I synthesis can legitimately report that an intervention has not been shown to work. The interval does not demonstrate harm, since most of its range lies above 0, and disagreement among trials would be quantified as heterogeneity rather than inferred from the interval.
rationales.eli10: Being the most reliable judge available does not obligate you to declare a winner. Here the most reliable available judge, a synthesis of randomized trials, is reporting that the true effect could be a small decline, no change, or a gain of over a point, and the data cannot distinguish among those. Whenever a confidence interval crosses zero, no difference stays on the table as a live possibility. That is a legitimate, high-quality result, and it is different from evidence of no effect: a wide interval like this one often signals that more or larger trials are needed.
