subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is a population in statistics?

rationales.whyCorrect: A population is the full group a question concerns.
rationales.eli10: It is everyone or everything we want to learn about.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is a sample?

rationales.whyCorrect: A sample supplies observations used to learn about a population.
rationales.eli10: It is a smaller scoop from a big group.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A numerical summary of a population is a:

rationales.whyCorrect: A parameter describes a population.
rationales.eli10: It is a number for the whole big group.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A numerical summary calculated from a sample is a:

rationales.whyCorrect: A statistic describes sample data.
rationales.eli10: It is a number from the smaller scoop.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is a variable?

rationales.whyCorrect: Variables take different values among observations.
rationales.eli10: It is something that can change from person to person.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is one recorded case or measurement called?

rationales.whyCorrect: An observation is one unit's recorded data.
rationales.eli10: It is one row in the information list.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Descriptive statistics mainly:

rationales.whyCorrect: They organize and describe a dataset.
rationales.eli10: They tell the data's short story.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Inferential statistics mainly:

rationales.whyCorrect: Inference uses sample evidence to estimate or test population claims.
rationales.eli10: A small scoop helps guess what is in the whole pot.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Evidence-based practice combines research evidence with:

rationales.whyCorrect: Responsible decisions integrate evidence, expertise, and individual priorities.
rationales.eli10: Good choices use studies, professional judgment, and what matters to the person.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A hospital wants average wait time for all visits. Which is the population?

rationales.whyCorrect: The target group is every visit covered by the question.
rationales.eli10: The big group includes all the visits being asked about.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A study records age in years. Age is the:

rationales.whyCorrect: Age varies among observed people.
rationales.eli10: Age is the changing fact in each row.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Researchers summarize 200 pulse rates with a median. This is:

rationales.whyCorrect: A median condenses the recorded sample values.
rationales.eli10: One middle number summarizes the list.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A sample mean estimates a population mean. The sample mean is a:

rationales.whyCorrect: It is calculated from sampled observations.
rationales.eli10: A number from the scoop estimates the whole pot.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why use a sample instead of measuring everyone?

rationales.whyCorrect: Sampling can reduce time, cost, and burden.
rationales.eli10: Checking a careful scoop is easier than checking the whole pot.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which question is statistical?

options.text: What is this patient's pulse now?
What is the average pulse among students?

rationales.whyCorrect: It anticipates variable data across a group.
rationales.eli10: Many students will have different pulses to summarize.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which practice protects health-data privacy?

rationales.whyCorrect: Removing direct identifiers reduces disclosure risk.
rationales.eli10: Take name tags off the data before sharing it.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A voluntary online survey overrepresents highly motivated people. This is:

rationales.whyCorrect: Self-selection can make respondents unlike the target population.
rationales.eli10: Only people eager to answer may give a lopsided scoop.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why should a data-collection rule be defined before a study?

rationales.whyCorrect: Standard rules reduce subjective and inconsistent measurement.
rationales.eli10: Everyone should use the same ruler from the start.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Missing values occur mostly among very ill participants. Why is this concerning?

rationales.whyCorrect: Systematic missingness can distort the observed sample.
rationales.eli10: The missing pieces come from one important part of the picture.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A chart reports 60 of 100 participants improved. What descriptive proportion is this?

rationales.eli10: Sixty out of one hundred means sixty percent.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which source best supports a clinical claim?

options.text: A systematically evaluated body of relevant research

rationales.whyCorrect: Synthesized relevant evidence is stronger than unsupported impressions.
rationales.eli10: Many carefully checked clues beat one story.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A sample differs from its population by chance. This is:

rationales.whyCorrect: Different random samples naturally yield different statistics.
rationales.eli10: Different scoops from soup contain slightly different pieces.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A researcher changes outcome definitions after seeing results. Main concern?

rationales.whyCorrect: Post hoc changes can favor attractive findings.
rationales.eli10: Moving the goal after seeing the score makes the game unfair.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why report units with health measurements?

rationales.whyCorrect: A value of 5 differs greatly if measured in mg versus g.
rationales.eli10: A number needs a label saying what it counts.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A sample of 1,000 is biased toward one clinic. What is the key limitation?

options.text: Size does not correct poor representativeness

rationales.whyCorrect: Systematic bias can persist despite many observations.
rationales.eli10: A giant scoop from one corner can still miss the whole pot.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which approach best estimates community vaccination rate?

rationales.whyCorrect: Probability sampling better represents the target community.
rationales.eli10: Choose names across the neighborhood, not just at one doorway.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A statistically precise estimate is ethically unusable because consent was absent. What principle applies?

rationales.whyCorrect: Scientific value does not erase participant rights.
rationales.eli10: A sharp answer is not acceptable if people were treated unfairly.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Two datasets share a mean but have different spreads. What follows?

rationales.whyCorrect: Variability adds information the mean cannot show.
rationales.eli10: The same average can hide very different piles of numbers.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A study question names exposure, outcome, and population. Why is this useful?

rationales.whyCorrect: Clear components align design and analysis with the objective.
rationales.eli10: A clear question tells you which clues to collect.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why should conclusions reflect study limitations?

rationales.whyCorrect: Acknowledging uncertainty keeps claims within the evidence.
rationales.eli10: Say how far the flashlight really shines.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Blood type is what kind of data?

rationales.whyCorrect: Blood groups are categories without ranking.
rationales.eli10: The labels differ but do not line up from low to high.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Pain rated mild, moderate, or severe is:

rationales.whyCorrect: The categories have a meaningful order.
rationales.eli10: The labels climb in order even without equal steps.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Number of clinic visits is:

rationales.whyCorrect: Visits are counted in whole numbers.
rationales.eli10: You count visits rather than measure pieces of one.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Body temperature measured precisely is:

rationales.whyCorrect: Temperature can take values along a continuum.
rationales.eli10: It can fall between ruler marks.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which scale has equal intervals but no true zero?

rationales.whyCorrect: Celsius temperature has meaningful differences but arbitrary zero.
rationales.eli10: Zero does not mean no temperature exists.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which measurement is ratio level?

rationales.whyCorrect: Mass has equal units and a meaningful zero.
rationales.eli10: Zero mass means none, so twice as much makes sense.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: In an experiment, the manipulated factor is the:

rationales.whyCorrect: Researchers assign or change the independent variable.
rationales.eli10: It is the knob the study turns.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: The measured response is the:

rationales.whyCorrect: The dependent variable is the outcome.
rationales.eli10: It is what the study watches afterward.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A confounder is related to both:

rationales.whyCorrect: It can create or distort an observed exposure-outcome relationship.
rationales.eli10: A third factor may tug both things being compared.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Researchers observe diet and blood pressure without assigning diet. This is:

rationales.whyCorrect: Exposure is recorded rather than experimentally assigned.
rationales.eli10: The researchers watch choices instead of choosing them.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Participants are randomly assigned to exercise programs. This is:

rationales.whyCorrect: Assignment of an intervention makes the design experimental.
rationales.eli10: The study chooses which program each person gets.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A study measures exposure and outcome at one time. It is:

rationales.whyCorrect: Cross-sectional designs provide a time-point snapshot.
rationales.eli10: It takes one picture of everyone now.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A cohort study typically groups people by:

rationales.whyCorrect: Cohorts track exposed and unexposed groups over time.
rationales.eli10: Start with a possible cause and watch what happens.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A case-control study begins by selecting people based on:

rationales.whyCorrect: Cases have the outcome; controls do not, then prior exposures are compared.
rationales.eli10: Start with who has the condition and look backward for clues.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Random assignment primarily helps balance:

rationales.whyCorrect: Chance assignment reduces systematic baseline differences.
rationales.eli10: Shuffling helps make fair starting teams.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Blinding outcome assessors mainly reduces:

rationales.whyCorrect: Unaware assessors are less likely to rate groups differently.
rationales.eli10: The scorer cannot favor a team they cannot identify.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Height in centimeters is best classified as:

rationales.whyCorrect: Height is measured continuously with a meaningful zero.
rationales.eli10: It uses a ruler and can include fractions.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A yes/no smoking variable is:

rationales.whyCorrect: It has two categories rather than numerical magnitude.
rationales.eli10: There are two labeled boxes.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why is patient ID nominal even when written as digits?

options.text: The digits label rather than measure
IDs have a true arithmetic zero

rationales.whyCorrect: Arithmetic on identification labels has no meaning.
rationales.eli10: A jersey number names a player; it does not measure them.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A study follows nurses for ten years to relate shift work to disease. It is a:

rationales.whyCorrect: Exposure is identified and outcomes are observed prospectively.
rationales.eli10: Group people by work pattern and watch forward.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Researchers compare past exposure among people with and without a rare disease. Best design?

rationales.whyCorrect: Case-control studies efficiently examine rare outcomes.
rationales.eli10: Find the rare cases first, then look backward.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why might assigning a harmful exposure be unethical?

rationales.whyCorrect: Experiments must minimize harm and have acceptable risk-benefit balance.
rationales.eli10: A study cannot fairly make people face needless danger.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A placebo control helps separate treatment effect from:

rationales.whyCorrect: Comparison reveals changes not specific to the active intervention.
rationales.eli10: A look-alike comparison shows what happens without the active ingredient.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Double blinding means which parties are unaware of assignment?

rationales.whyCorrect: Masking both reduces expectation-related behavior and assessment bias.
rationales.eli10: Neither the receiver nor the main scorer knows the team.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Income categories low, middle, high are:

rationales.whyCorrect: The categories have order without defined equal distances.
rationales.eli10: They line up, but the gaps are not measured evenly.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A confounder is controlled in analysis. The goal is to:

rationales.whyCorrect: Adjustment reduces distortion from third variables.
rationales.eli10: Hold the extra tug steady to see the main link better.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why is a randomized trial strong for causal inference?

options.text: Assignment precedes outcome and balances confounders

rationales.whyCorrect: Randomization improves comparability before outcomes occur.
rationales.eli10: Fairly shuffled teams make the treatment the main planned difference.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A cross-sectional study finds exposure and disease together. Main limitation?

rationales.whyCorrect: A snapshot may not show which occurred first.
rationales.eli10: One photo cannot tell which event came before.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A measurement tool gives the same wrong value repeatedly. It is:

rationales.whyCorrect: Consistency indicates reliability; inaccuracy indicates poor validity.
rationales.eli10: The ruler repeats itself but marks the wrong length.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which design best tests a prevention program while respecting uncertainty?

rationales.whyCorrect: Ethical randomization and comparison can estimate program effects.
rationales.eli10: Fair teams and safety watchers give a strong test.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A frequency table lists:

rationales.whyCorrect: Frequencies show how often each value occurs.
rationales.eli10: It counts how many items fit each box.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Relative frequency is:

rationales.whyCorrect: It expresses a category's share of all observations.
rationales.eli10: Divide a box's count by the whole pile.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Cumulative frequency is a:

rationales.whyCorrect: It adds frequencies through an ordered value.
rationales.eli10: Keep adding each row to the earlier total.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which graph best compares blood-type categories?

rationales.whyCorrect: Separated bars suit unordered categorical counts.
rationales.eli10: Use one bar for each named group.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which graph displays a continuous distribution?

rationales.whyCorrect: Touching histogram bins show frequencies across numeric intervals.
rationales.eli10: Neighboring number ranges become touching bars.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which graph best shows change over time?

rationales.whyCorrect: Connected points reveal temporal trends.
rationales.eli10: A line lets your eye follow the story through time.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which graph shows relationships between two quantitative variables?

rationales.whyCorrect: Each point pairs one x value with one y value.
rationales.eli10: Dots show how two measurements travel together.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A box plot displays:

rationales.whyCorrect: Its box and whiskers summarize position and spread.
rationales.eli10: It shows the middle, the box of central values, and unusual points.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What should every graph axis include?

rationales.whyCorrect: Labels define what values represent.
rationales.eli10: Tell readers what each ruler measures.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A pie chart is most appropriate for:

rationales.whyCorrect: Slices represent category proportions summing to 100%.
rationales.eli10: Cut the whole pie into group shares.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A histogram differs from a bar graph because histogram bars:

options.text: Represent numeric intervals and usually touch

rationales.whyCorrect: Continuous bins are adjacent, unlike separate categories.
rationales.eli10: Number neighborhoods meet, so their bars meet.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A y-axis starts at 98 rather than 0. What risk arises?

rationales.whyCorrect: A truncated scale magnifies visual separation.
rationales.eli10: Zooming the ruler can make a tiny gap look huge.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which display best shows monthly infection counts for a year?

rationales.whyCorrect: Ordered monthly points show trends and changes.
rationales.eli10: Connect each month's count to follow the year.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which display best compares median stays across four hospitals?

rationales.whyCorrect: Comparable box plots show center, spread, and outliers for each hospital.
rationales.eli10: Four boxes let you compare middles and ranges.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: In a scatterplot, an upward pattern indicates:

rationales.whyCorrect: Higher x values tend to accompany higher y values.
rationales.eli10: The dots climb as you move right.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why should categories in a pie chart be mutually exclusive?

options.text: So shares do not overlap-count the whole

rationales.whyCorrect: Each observation should contribute to one slice.
rationales.eli10: One piece should not be counted in two slices.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A frequency is 15 in a sample of 60. Relative frequency?

rationales.eli10: Fifteen is one quarter of sixty.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Frequencies 2, 3, 5 have what final cumulative frequency?

rationales.whyCorrect: The running total is 2+3+5=10.
rationales.eli10: Add every box to count the whole list.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which graph best displays age distribution for 500 adults?

rationales.whyCorrect: Age is quantitative and suited to interval bins.
rationales.eli10: Group nearby ages into touching bars.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A graph uses unequal time gaps spaced equally. Why misleading?

options.text: Visual distances no longer match time distances

rationales.whyCorrect: Equal spacing falsely implies equal time intervals.
rationales.eli10: The paper ruler lies about how much time passed.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why include sample size with percentages?

options.text: It gives context for stability and counts

rationales.whyCorrect: 50% of 4 differs in precision from 50% of 4,000.
rationales.eli10: Half of a tiny group is less steady than half of a huge group.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A box plot has a long upper whisker. This suggests:

rationales.whyCorrect: A longer high-value tail indicates right skew.
rationales.eli10: The number trail stretches farther to the high side.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which table entry helps detect data-entry errors?

rationales.whyCorrect: Unexpected values stand out when counts are summarized.
rationales.eli10: A strange box like age 500 is easy to spot.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A legend is essential when:

rationales.whyCorrect: Legends map colors or symbols to groups.
rationales.eli10: It is the key explaining which mark belongs to which team.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A hospital compares event counts, but departments differ greatly in size. Better display?

rationales.whyCorrect: Rates support fair comparison across different exposure sizes.
rationales.eli10: Compare events per equal number of chances.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why avoid 3-D effects in bar charts?

options.text: They convert data to ratio scale

rationales.whyCorrect: Depth and angle make values harder to judge accurately.
rationales.eli10: Fancy tilted blocks can fool your eyes about height.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A disease dashboard shows cases but not population size. Main problem?

rationales.whyCorrect: Counts without denominators do not represent population rates.
rationales.eli10: Ten cases mean something different in a town of 100 versus a million.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which display combines individual values and distribution shape for a small sample?

rationales.whyCorrect: A dot plot preserves each observation while revealing clusters and gaps.
rationales.eli10: Stack one dot for every value so none disappear.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Two graphs use different y-axis scales. What should a reviewer do?

options.text: Compare numerical scales before visual slopes

rationales.whyCorrect: Scale differences can create false visual contrasts.
rationales.eli10: Check both rulers before judging the hills.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why pair a visualization with accessible text or a data table?

options.text: To support readers who cannot use the visual alone

rationales.whyCorrect: Alternative representations improve accurate and equitable interpretation.
rationales.eli10: Give another doorway to the same information.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: The mean is calculated by:

options.text: Summing values and dividing by count

rationales.whyCorrect: The arithmetic mean distributes the total equally.
rationales.eli10: Add the numbers and share equally among them.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: The median is the:

rationales.whyCorrect: Half the observations lie on each side of the median.
rationales.eli10: Line numbers up and find the center seat.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: The mode is the:

rationales.whyCorrect: The mode occurs most often.
rationales.eli10: It is the number that shows up the most.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which center is least affected by an extreme outlier?

rationales.whyCorrect: The median depends on order, not outlier magnitude.
rationales.eli10: A giant end number barely moves the middle seat.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: The 75th percentile means:

options.text: 75% of values are at or below it

rationales.whyCorrect: Percentiles locate a value within an ordered distribution.
rationales.eli10: Three quarters of the group are no higher than that mark.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Quartiles divide ordered data into:

rationales.whyCorrect: Q1, Q2, and Q3 mark four equal-count sections.
rationales.eli10: Three cuts divide the line into four groups.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: The second quartile equals the:

rationales.whyCorrect: Q2 is the 50th percentile.
rationales.eli10: The halfway quartile is the middle.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A weighted mean gives:

rationales.whyCorrect: Weights reflect differing importance or frequency.
rationales.eli10: Some scores count more heavily in the final average.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: For 2, 4, 6, the mean is:

rationales.eli10: Twelve shared among three values is four.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: For 1, 3, 8, 20, the median is:

rationales.whyCorrect: With four values, average the middle two: (3+8)/2=5.5.
rationales.eli10: The middle lies halfway between the two center seats.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: For 2, 2, 3, 5, the mode is:

rationales.whyCorrect: Two occurs more often than other values.
rationales.eli10: The repeated winner is two.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A salary distribution has a few extremely high values. Best typical center?

rationales.whyCorrect: The median resists upward pull from extreme salaries.
rationales.eli10: A few huge paychecks cannot drag the middle person far.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Mean wait time is 20 minutes for 10 visits. Total wait time?

rationales.whyCorrect: Total = mean × count = 20×10.
rationales.eli10: Ten groups of twenty minutes make two hundred.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Scores 70 and 90 have equal weight. Their mean is:

rationales.eli10: The halfway point between seventy and ninety is eighty.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A course grade is 40% exam 80 and 60% clinical 90. Weighted mean?

rationales.eli10: Count the ninety more heavily because it has the bigger weight.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A value at the 90th percentile is higher than approximately:

rationales.whyCorrect: About nine tenths of observations lie at or below it.
rationales.eli10: It stands above roughly nine out of ten values.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why can mean and median differ greatly?

options.text: Skew or outliers pull the mean

rationales.whyCorrect: Extreme tails affect the arithmetic mean more strongly.
rationales.eli10: A long tail tugs the balancing point away from the middle seat.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: If every value increases by 5, the mean:

rationales.whyCorrect: Adding a constant shifts the total by 5 per observation.
rationales.eli10: Move every block five steps and the balance point moves five steps.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which center can describe nominal blood types?

rationales.whyCorrect: The most frequent category is meaningful for nominal data.
rationales.eli10: You can name the most common label.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A median of 12 days means:

options.text: Half the ordered stays are on each side

rationales.whyCorrect: The median marks the distribution's middle position.
rationales.eli10: Twelve sits at the middle of the lined-up stays.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A dataset has values 4, 4, 9, 9. It is:

rationales.whyCorrect: Both 4 and 9 share highest frequency.
rationales.eli10: Two numbers tie as most common.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which statistic identifies a person's relative standing?

rationales.whyCorrect: Percentile rank compares a value with the ordered group.
rationales.eli10: It says how many classmates scored no higher.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: After adding a very high outlier, which changes more?

rationales.whyCorrect: The mean incorporates the outlier's magnitude.
rationales.eli10: A huge number pulls the arithmetic balance point hardest.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why report both median and IQR for skewed stays?

options.text: They robustly summarize center and spread

rationales.whyCorrect: Both resist distortion from long tails.
rationales.eli10: Use sturdy middle measures when a few stays are enormous.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A mean of binary outcomes coded 1=yes, 0=no equals the:

rationales.whyCorrect: The sum counts yes outcomes; dividing by total gives their proportion.
rationales.eli10: Average zeros and ones to get the share of ones.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A class mean is 80 for 20 students, then a score 100 is added. New mean?

rationales.whyCorrect: Original total 1600 plus 100 equals 1700; 1700/21≈81.0.
rationales.eli10: Add the new score to the pile, then share among twenty-one.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Group A has mean 70 (n=10), Group B mean 80 (n=30). Combined mean?

rationales.eli10: The larger eighty group pulls the combined average closer to eighty.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why is averaging subgroup means without sizes risky?

rationales.whyCorrect: Small and large groups should not contribute equally unless sizes match.
rationales.eli10: A class of thirty should count more than a class of three.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: If Q1=10 and Q3=22, what share lies between them?

rationales.whyCorrect: The interval from Q1 to Q3 contains the middle half.
rationales.eli10: The quartile box holds the middle two quarters.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which report best characterizes a multimodal dataset?

options.text: Name multiple modes and describe distribution

rationales.whyCorrect: Several peaks may represent meaningful subgroups hidden by one center.
rationales.eli10: Tell readers about each hill, not just one balancing point.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: The range equals:

rationales.whyCorrect: Range uses the two extreme observations.
rationales.eli10: Subtract the smallest number from the largest.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Variance summarizes average:

rationales.whyCorrect: Squaring deviations measures overall spread around the mean.
rationales.eli10: It averages squared distances from the balance point.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Standard deviation is the:

rationales.whyCorrect: Taking the square root returns variability to original units.
rationales.eli10: It turns squared spread back into the measurement's units.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: The interquartile range equals:

rationales.whyCorrect: IQR spans the middle 50% of observations.
rationales.eli10: Subtract the first quartile from the third.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A small standard deviation means values are:

rationales.whyCorrect: Less average distance from the mean yields lower SD.
rationales.eli10: The numbers huddle near their balance point.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A normal distribution is:

rationales.whyCorrect: A normal curve is symmetric around its mean.
rationales.eli10: It looks like an even hill.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Right skew means the longer tail points:

rationales.whyCorrect: A few high values stretch the right side.
rationales.eli10: The number trail reaches toward bigger values.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A z score reports distance from the mean in:

rationales.whyCorrect: z=(value−mean)/SD standardizes position.
rationales.eli10: It counts how many usual spread-steps away a value sits.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A z score of 0 identifies a value at the:

rationales.whyCorrect: Subtracting the mean gives zero.
rationales.eli10: Zero steps away means right at the average.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Data 4, 7, 10 have range:

rationales.eli10: The end-to-end distance is six.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Two groups share a mean; Group A has larger SD. Group A is:

rationales.whyCorrect: Higher SD indicates greater spread about the mean.
rationales.eli10: Its numbers wander farther from the middle.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why is IQR preferred with strong outliers?

rationales.whyCorrect: IQR depends on quartiles rather than endpoints.
rationales.eli10: The middle box ignores how far wild ends stretch.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A value is 80, mean 70, SD 5. Its z score is:

rationales.eli10: Ten points above is two five-point steps.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A z score of −1.5 means the value is:

rationales.whyCorrect: The negative sign indicates below the mean.
rationales.eli10: It sits one and a half usual steps below average.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: If every value is identical, standard deviation is:

rationales.whyCorrect: All deviations from the mean are zero.
rationales.eli10: No number wanders from the center.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Adding 10 to every score changes SD how?

rationales.whyCorrect: Shifting all values equally does not change distances among them.
rationales.eli10: Move the whole crowd together and its spread stays the same.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Multiplying every value by 2 makes SD:

rationales.whyCorrect: Scale changes multiply standard deviations by the absolute factor.
rationales.eli10: Stretch the ruler twice and all distances double.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: In a normal distribution, about 68% lies within:

rationales.whyCorrect: The empirical rule places about 68% within ±1 SD.
rationales.eli10: About two thirds fit in the hill's central step.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which shape usually has mean greater than median?

rationales.whyCorrect: High tail values pull the mean rightward.
rationales.eli10: Big end numbers tug the average above the middle seat.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A box-plot point lies beyond 1.5 IQR from a quartile. It is flagged as:

rationales.whyCorrect: The 1.5-IQR rule identifies unusually distant observations.
rationales.eli10: It sits beyond the box plot's usual fence.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why should an outlier be investigated before removal?

options.text: It may be valid or reveal error

rationales.whyCorrect: The value may carry information or reflect a correctable mistake.
rationales.eli10: Check whether the strange dot is a gem or a typo.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Group X: SD 2; Group Y: SD 10, same units. Which is more consistent?

rationales.whyCorrect: Lower SD means observations are closer together.
rationales.eli10: X's numbers form the tighter bunch.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A distribution is symmetric with mean 50. What is likely median?

rationales.whyCorrect: In a symmetric unimodal distribution, mean and median coincide.
rationales.eli10: An even hill balances at its middle.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why can range be unstable across samples?

options.text: It depends only on two extremes

rationales.whyCorrect: One unusual minimum or maximum can alter it greatly.
rationales.eli10: The whole answer rests on the two end numbers.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A z score permits comparison of different tests because it:

rationales.whyCorrect: Standardization places scores on a common relative scale.
rationales.eli10: It converts different rulers into usual-step distances.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Two tests: score 90, mean 80, SD 5; score 50, mean 40, SD 10. Better relative performance?

rationales.whyCorrect: z scores are 2 and 1, so the first ranks higher.
rationales.eli10: The first is two usual steps above average versus one.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A dataset has mean 20 and variance 9. Standard deviation?

rationales.whyCorrect: The square root of 9 is 3.
rationales.eli10: Undo the square to get three.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A bimodal distribution has high SD. What should be checked?

options.text: Whether distinct subgroups create the spread

rationales.whyCorrect: Pooled groups can inflate spread and obscure separate centers.
rationales.eli10: Two hills may look like one very wide crowd.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why report distribution shape with mean and SD?

options.text: Mean and SD can hide skew or multiple peaks

rationales.whyCorrect: Shape determines whether these summaries represent data well.
rationales.eli10: A center and spread do not show whether the pile has a long tail.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: For heavily skewed lengths of stay, best paired summary?

rationales.whyCorrect: Median and IQR robustly represent skewed data.
rationales.eli10: Use the sturdy middle seat and middle box.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Probability values range from:

rationales.whyCorrect: Zero means impossible and one means certain.
rationales.eli10: Chance runs from no chance to sure.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Probability 0.25 equals:

rationales.whyCorrect: Multiplying by 100 converts proportion to percent.
rationales.eli10: A quarter chance is twenty-five percent.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: The complement of probability 0.30 is:

rationales.eli10: What is left after thirty percent is seventy percent.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Independent events are events where:

options.text: One does not change the other's probability

rationales.whyCorrect: Knowledge of one event does not alter the other event's chance.
rationales.eli10: One coin flip does not boss the next flip.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Mutually exclusive events:

rationales.whyCorrect: They share no outcomes in a single trial.
rationales.eli10: One draw cannot be both red and blue at once.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Conditional probability is probability of A:

rationales.whyCorrect: It updates chance using a stated condition.
rationales.eli10: It asks the chance after learning a clue.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: If independent event chances are 0.5 and 0.2, chance both occur?

rationales.whyCorrect: Multiply independent probabilities: 0.5×0.2=0.10.
rationales.eli10: Half of one fifth is one tenth.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: If mutually exclusive event chances are 0.3 and 0.4, chance either?

rationales.whyCorrect: Add disjoint probabilities: 0.3+0.4=0.7.
rationales.eli10: Separate chances can be added.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Absolute risk is:

options.text: Risk in exposed divided by control

rationales.whyCorrect: It directly states how many experience an outcome.
rationales.eli10: It is the event share within one group.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Relative risk compares:

options.text: Risk in one group to risk in another

rationales.whyCorrect: RR is a ratio of group risks.
rationales.eli10: It asks how many times as likely one group is.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Risk is 20% with exposure and 10% without. Relative risk?

rationales.eli10: Twenty percent is twice ten percent.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: For the same groups, absolute risk increase is:

rationales.eli10: Subtract ten percent from twenty percent.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Odds of an event equal:

rationales.whyCorrect: Odds compare occurrence probability with nonoccurrence probability.
rationales.eli10: Compare yes chances with no chances.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: If risk is 0.20, odds are:

rationales.eli10: One chance of yes for four chances of no is one quarter.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A test result changes disease probability. This illustrates:

rationales.whyCorrect: Post-test probability conditions on the observed result.
rationales.eli10: A new clue updates the chance.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why can relative risk sound more dramatic than absolute risk?

rationales.whyCorrect: A large ratio may reflect very small underlying risks.
rationales.eli10: Doubling a tiny chance can still leave a tiny chance.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Risk falls from 4% to 2%. Relative risk reduction?

rationales.eli10: The risk was cut in half.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Same change: absolute risk reduction?

rationales.whyCorrect: 4%−2%=2 percentage points.
rationales.eli10: Only two people per hundred fewer have the event.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Two events each have probability 0.5 but are mutually exclusive. Chance either?

rationales.whyCorrect: Their disjoint probabilities sum to one.
rationales.eli10: The two separate halves fill the whole.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why are repeated coin flips independent?

options.text: One outcome does not alter the next flip's chance
They are mutually exclusive across flips

rationales.whyCorrect: With stable conditions, previous results do not affect the next trial.
rationales.eli10: The coin has no memory.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A screening program tests higher-risk people. Positive predictive value changes because:

options.text: It depends partly on disease prevalence

rationales.whyCorrect: Predictive values vary with pretest prevalence.
rationales.eli10: A clue means more when the condition is common in the tested group.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A 1-in-1,000 risk is best communicated as:

rationales.whyCorrect: Using absolute frequency and percent improves understanding.
rationales.eli10: Say the same chance with both a crowd picture and a percent.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A risk ratio of 1 suggests:

rationales.whyCorrect: The numerator and denominator risks are equal.
rationales.eli10: Both groups have the same event share.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which statement confuses association with certainty?

options.text: Everyone exposed will develop the outcome

rationales.whyCorrect: A group-level probability does not determine each individual's result.
rationales.eli10: A higher chance is not a promise about every person.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A study reports RR=3 but risks are 0.03% vs 0.01%. Best interpretation?

rationales.whyCorrect: Both relative and small absolute changes should be reported.
rationales.eli10: Three times sounds big, but the crowd difference is only two per ten thousand.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: If P(A)=0.6, P(B)=0.5, and P(A and B)=0.3, events are:

rationales.whyCorrect: 0.6×0.5=0.3, satisfying independence.
rationales.eli10: The together chance equals the product of separate chances.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why are mutually exclusive events with positive probabilities not independent?

options.text: Occurrence of one makes the other impossible

rationales.whyCorrect: Knowing one occurred changes the other's probability to zero.
rationales.eli10: Choosing one door means the other door was not chosen.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A sample finds zero events among 20 people. Can true risk be declared zero?

options.text: No; a small sample may miss rare events

rationales.whyCorrect: Absence in limited observations does not prove impossibility.
rationales.eli10: Twenty quiet tries may simply miss a rare event.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why use natural frequencies when explaining test results?

options.text: They clarify joint and conditional counts

rationales.whyCorrect: Concrete counts often make probability relationships easier to see.
rationales.eli10: People can picture ten cases among one thousand better than nested percentages.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A risk estimate has wide uncertainty. What communication is best?

options.text: Report the range and explain uncertainty

rationales.whyCorrect: Intervals prevent false precision and show plausible values.
rationales.eli10: Show the fuzzy edges, not just the center dot.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Simple random sampling gives each population member:

rationales.whyCorrect: Equal random selection reduces systematic selection differences.
rationales.eli10: Every name gets an equal lottery ticket.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Convenience sampling selects people who are:

rationales.whyCorrect: Convenience prioritizes access over representativeness.
rationales.eli10: It asks whoever is nearby.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Stratified sampling first divides the population into:

rationales.whyCorrect: Random samples are taken within defined strata.
rationales.eli10: Make important group boxes, then sample each box.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Systematic sampling might select:

options.text: Every tenth name after a random start

rationales.whyCorrect: A fixed interval defines systematic selection.
rationales.eli10: Start somewhere by chance, then count every tenth.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Cluster sampling selects:

rationales.whyCorrect: Clusters such as schools are sampled, then members within them are studied.
rationales.eli10: Pick whole neighborhoods instead of scattered houses.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Sampling bias occurs when:

rationales.whyCorrect: Some population members are consistently over- or underrepresented.
rationales.eli10: The scoop repeatedly misses one part of the pot.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Selection bias threatens comparison when groups differ because of:

rationales.whyCorrect: Enrollment or retention processes may create baseline differences.
rationales.eli10: The doorway puts different kinds of people on each team.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Recall bias arises from differences in:

rationales.whyCorrect: Cases and controls may remember exposure differently.
rationales.eli10: Memory does not replay the past perfectly.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Measurement bias is systematic error in:

rationales.whyCorrect: A flawed instrument or procedure can shift measurements consistently.
rationales.eli10: A crooked ruler bends every answer.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Confounding occurs when a third factor:

rationales.whyCorrect: It can partially or fully explain an observed association.
rationales.eli10: A hidden string pulls both puppets.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Internal validity concerns whether:

options.text: The study's effect estimate is credible for participants

rationales.whyCorrect: Internal validity depends on control of bias and confounding within the study.
rationales.eli10: Did the study fairly answer its own question?

subjectWideQuestions.stem: External validity concerns:

rationales.whyCorrect: It asks whether findings apply to other people and settings.
rationales.eli10: Will the answer travel outside this study room?

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Reliability means a measure is:

rationales.whyCorrect: Reliable measurements reproduce under similar conditions.
rationales.eli10: The ruler gives the same answer again.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Validity means a tool:

options.text: Measures what it intends to measure

rationales.whyCorrect: Validity concerns accuracy of the intended construct.
rationales.eli10: The ruler measures the right thing.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A blood-pressure device repeatedly reads 10 mmHg high. It is:

rationales.whyCorrect: A stable offset is consistent yet inaccurate.
rationales.eli10: It repeats the same mistake.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Random sampling primarily supports:

rationales.whyCorrect: Probability selection improves generalizability.
rationales.eli10: A fair scoop better resembles the pot.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Random assignment primarily supports:

rationales.whyCorrect: Assignment balances confounders between study arms.
rationales.eli10: Shuffling makes fair teams.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Only 20% of invited people respond. Main concern?

rationales.whyCorrect: Respondents may differ systematically from nonrespondents.
rationales.eli10: The people who answer may not resemble those who stay silent.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Participants drop out more often from one treatment. This can cause:

rationales.whyCorrect: Differential loss can destroy group comparability.
rationales.eli10: One team loses a special kind of player.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A survey asks, “How helpful was our excellent service?” This risks:

rationales.whyCorrect: The positive wording nudges answers.
rationales.eli10: The question whispers which answer it wants.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why pilot-test a questionnaire?

rationales.whyCorrect: Small preliminary testing reveals measurement problems.
rationales.eli10: Try the ruler before measuring everyone.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A scale is recalibrated before each clinic session. This reduces:

rationales.whyCorrect: Calibration maintains a stable measurement standard.
rationales.eli10: Reset the ruler so it does not slowly slide wrong.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A study excludes non-English speakers. Which issue is most direct?

rationales.whyCorrect: Results may not apply to the excluded population.
rationales.eli10: The flashlight did not shine on that group.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why oversample a small important subgroup in stratified sampling?

rationales.whyCorrect: Extra cases can support precise subgroup analysis, with weighting for totals.
rationales.eli10: Take a bigger scoop from a tiny section so you can study it.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A random sample has a 5% response rate. Is random selection alone enough?

options.text: No; nonresponse can still bias results

rationales.whyCorrect: Selection benefits can be lost when response differs systematically.
rationales.eli10: A fair invitation does not ensure a fair group of answerers.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Blinded assessors use an invalid tool. What remains wrong?

rationales.whyCorrect: Blinding cannot make the instrument measure the intended construct.
rationales.eli10: Covering the scorer's eyes cannot fix a crooked ruler.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A confounder is matched in design. Why adjust for it again cautiously?

rationales.whyCorrect: Matching may be incomplete and must be reflected in analysis.
rationales.eli10: Even paired teams may have small leftover differences.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why can a very precise biased estimate be misleading?

options.text: It can be tightly centered on the wrong value

rationales.whyCorrect: Low random error does not correct systematic error.
rationales.eli10: Many darts can form a tight group away from the target.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which combination best supports generalizable causal evidence?

options.text: Representative recruitment plus valid randomized comparison

rationales.whyCorrect: Representation aids external validity; randomization aids internal validity.
rationales.eli10: Use a fair audience and fair teams.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Ethical sampling requires fair inclusion because:

options.text: Every group must have equal outcomes
Burdens and benefits should not be unjustly distributed

rationales.whyCorrect: Justice guides who bears risk and gains potential benefit.
rationales.eli10: Do not make one group carry all the risk while another gets all the help.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Correlation describes:

rationales.whyCorrect: Correlation summarizes how two quantitative variables vary together.
rationales.eli10: It tells whether two number trails move together.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A positive correlation means:

options.text: One rises as the other falls
Higher values tend to occur together

rationales.whyCorrect: The scatterplot generally slopes upward.
rationales.eli10: The dots climb from left to right.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A negative correlation means:

options.text: One variable rises as the other falls

rationales.whyCorrect: The variables tend to move in opposite directions.
rationales.eli10: One trail goes up while the other goes down.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A correlation near zero suggests:

rationales.whyCorrect: The data show little straight-line relationship.
rationales.eli10: The dots do not lean clearly up or down.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: The correlation coefficient r ranges from:

rationales.whyCorrect: Values near ±1 show strong linear association.
rationales.eli10: The ruler runs from perfect down to perfect up.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A scatterplot is used for:

rationales.whyCorrect: Each point represents paired numerical measurements.
rationales.eli10: Each dot carries an x number and a y number.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A regression line primarily supports:

options.text: Predicting an outcome from a predictor

rationales.whyCorrect: Regression models the expected outcome as predictor values change.
rationales.eli10: The line gives a best guess for y from x.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why does correlation not prove causation?

options.text: Confounding or reverse direction may explain it

rationales.whyCorrect: Association alone does not establish the causal pathway.
rationales.eli10: Two alarms can ring together because one hidden fire triggers both.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: An r of −0.90 indicates:

rationales.whyCorrect: Magnitude 0.90 is strong and the sign is negative.
rationales.eli10: The dots closely slope downward.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: An r of 0.15 indicates:

rationales.whyCorrect: The positive direction is slight because magnitude is near zero.
rationales.eli10: The dots lean upward only a little.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Hours studied and score have r=0.7. Best statement?

options.text: They show a moderately strong positive association

rationales.whyCorrect: The coefficient supports association, not individual certainty or causation.
rationales.eli10: More study often travels with higher scores, but it is not a promise.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: An outlier can affect correlation by:

rationales.whyCorrect: A distant influential point can alter the fitted pattern.
rationales.eli10: One faraway dot can tilt the whole line.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A curved relationship may have r near zero because:

rationales.whyCorrect: Positive and negative slopes within a curve can cancel linearly.
rationales.eli10: A clear U shape does not lean one straight way.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A regression slope of 2 means predicted outcome:

rationales.whyCorrect: The slope is expected change in outcome for a one-unit x increase.
rationales.eli10: One step right raises the line two steps.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is a residual?

rationales.whyCorrect: Residuals measure vertical deviations from the fitted line.
rationales.eli10: It is the gap between a dot and the prediction line.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A positive slope with p<0.05 establishes:

options.text: Evidence of linear association, not necessarily causation

rationales.whyCorrect: Significance addresses compatibility with a null slope under assumptions.
rationales.eli10: The line likely tilts, but why it tilts still needs evidence.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Ice-cream sales and sunburn both rise in summer. Likely confounder?

rationales.whyCorrect: Seasonal weather affects both variables.
rationales.eli10: Sunshine pulls both ice-cream buying and sunburn upward.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why avoid prediction far outside observed x values?

options.text: The relationship may not continue there

rationales.whyCorrect: Extrapolation assumes an unverified pattern beyond the data.
rationales.eli10: The drawn road may turn after the map ends.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which plot suggests homoscedastic residuals?

options.text: Similar residual spread across fitted values

rationales.whyCorrect: Constant variance appears as roughly even vertical scatter.
rationales.eli10: The prediction errors stay equally wide along the line.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A perfect correlation can still be noncausal when:

options.text: Both are driven by a third variable

rationales.whyCorrect: A deterministic common cause can generate perfect association.
rationales.eli10: One puppeteer can move two puppets exactly together.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Two variables have r=−0.6. Which transformation changes the sign?

options.text: Change units from kg to g

rationales.whyCorrect: Reversing one scale reverses association direction.
rationales.eli10: Flip one ruler and down becomes up.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why inspect a scatterplot before reporting r?

options.text: It reveals curves, clusters, and influential points

rationales.whyCorrect: A single coefficient can hide important structure.
rationales.eli10: Look at the dot picture before trusting one summary number.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A model predicts pulse from age. Age's coefficient is −0.3. Interpretation?

options.text: Predicted pulse falls 0.3 units per year

rationales.whyCorrect: The coefficient describes average modeled change, assuming model conditions.
rationales.eli10: The line drops three-tenths for each step in age.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Adding a confounder to regression greatly reduces an association. This suggests:

rationales.whyCorrect: Adjustment separated some third-variable influence.
rationales.eli10: After holding one puppet string, the main link weakened.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A narrow prediction interval means:

options.text: Predictions are relatively precise under the model

rationales.whyCorrect: Narrower ranges represent less modeled uncertainty.
rationales.eli10: The model's guess has smaller fuzzy edges.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Two subgroups each show positive association, but pooled data show negative. This illustrates:

rationales.whyCorrect: Different subgroup locations can create Simpson's paradox.
rationales.eli10: Mixing two teams can flip the story seen within each team.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why can measurement error weaken correlation?

rationales.whyCorrect: Unreliable values add unrelated variation.
rationales.eli10: A shaky ruler blurs how two trails move together.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A high r with a tiny predictor range should be interpreted cautiously because:

options.text: Restriction can make association unstable or unrepresentative

rationales.whyCorrect: Limited range may not reflect the broader relationship.
rationales.eli10: A short road segment may not show the whole road.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which analysis best separates association from causal claim?

options.text: Combine design evidence, timing, and confounder control

rationales.whyCorrect: Causality requires more evidence than covariance.
rationales.eli10: Ask who came first and whether hidden strings were controlled.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A regression fits well on training data but poorly on new data. Likely issue?

rationales.whyCorrect: The model captured sample noise rather than stable structure.
rationales.eli10: It memorized one worksheet instead of learning the rule.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: The null hypothesis usually states:

rationales.whyCorrect: It supplies a reference claim for testing.
rationales.eli10: Start by pretending there is no real difference.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: The alternative hypothesis states:

rationales.whyCorrect: It represents the competing research claim.
rationales.eli10: It says a real difference may be there.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A p value is calculated assuming:

options.text: The null hypothesis and model assumptions

rationales.whyCorrect: It assesses data extremeness under the null model.
rationales.eli10: Ask how surprising the data are if no real effect exists.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: At α=0.05, p=0.03 is called:

rationales.whyCorrect: The p value falls below the prespecified threshold.
rationales.eli10: The result crossed the study's surprise line.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A Type I error is:

options.text: Failing to reject a false null

rationales.whyCorrect: It is a false-positive conclusion.
rationales.eli10: The alarm rings when no real fire exists.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A Type II error is:

options.text: Failing to reject a false null

rationales.whyCorrect: It is a false-negative testing outcome.
rationales.eli10: A real fire is present, but the alarm stays quiet.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Statistical power is probability of:

rationales.whyCorrect: Power equals 1−Type II error probability for a chosen effect.
rationales.eli10: It is the alarm's chance of catching a real fire.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A 95% confidence interval provides:

options.text: A range from a repeated-sampling method

rationales.whyCorrect: The procedure captures the true parameter in 95% of repeated studies under assumptions.
rationales.eli10: A method that usually builds nets covering the true value.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Larger samples generally produce:

rationales.whyCorrect: Standard errors shrink as information increases.
rationales.eli10: More measurements sharpen the estimate's fuzzy edges.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Clinical significance concerns:

rationales.whyCorrect: An effect can be statistically clear yet too small to matter.
rationales.eli10: Ask whether the difference actually helps in real life.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A p value of 0.20 means:

options.text: The null has 20% chance of truth
Data are not unusual enough to reject at 0.05

rationales.whyCorrect: Failure to reach significance is not proof of no effect.
rationales.eli10: The clue was not strong enough, but absence is not proven.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A 95% CI for a mean difference is −2 to 5. At 0.05, it:

options.text: Includes no difference, so is not significant

rationales.whyCorrect: Zero is a plausible value under the interval method.
rationales.eli10: The net still covers the no-change point.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A 95% CI for risk ratio is 1.2 to 2.0. It indicates:

rationales.whyCorrect: The interval excludes the null ratio of 1.
rationales.eli10: The whole net sits above the equal-risk mark.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Increasing sample size while effect stays fixed generally increases:

rationales.whyCorrect: More information makes true effects easier to detect.
rationales.eli10: A bigger flashlight can spot a small real object.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why prespecify α and outcomes?

rationales.whyCorrect: Advance rules reduce data-driven favorable selection.
rationales.eli10: Set the finish line before the race starts.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A huge study finds a 0.1-unit difference with p<0.001. Main question?

rationales.whyCorrect: Large samples can make trivial effects statistically significant.
rationales.eli10: A tiny difference can be clear but not useful.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A small study has a wide CI around no effect. Best conclusion?

options.text: Evidence is inconclusive, not proof of equality

rationales.whyCorrect: Wide uncertainty allows important benefit or harm.
rationales.eli10: The flashlight is too fuzzy to see the answer well.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Testing 20 outcomes without correction increases:

options.text: Chance of at least one Type I error

rationales.whyCorrect: Multiple opportunities raise false-positive risk.
rationales.eli10: More alarm buttons create more chances for one false ring.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A result is significant but study is biased. What follows?

options.text: The p value does not rescue validity

rationales.whyCorrect: Significance calculations do not correct systematic design error.
rationales.eli10: Precise math cannot straighten a crooked ruler.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which change reduces Type II error?

rationales.whyCorrect: Greater information improves detection of true effects.
rationales.eli10: More clear clues help the alarm notice a real fire.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why report effect size with p value?

options.text: It shows magnitude, not just compatibility with null

rationales.whyCorrect: Decision-making needs the size and uncertainty of effects.
rationales.eli10: Tell how big the difference is, not only whether it crossed a line.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A CI is 2 to 4 units. Best point estimate is often near:

rationales.whyCorrect: Many symmetric intervals center on the estimate at 3.
rationales.eli10: The dot sits near the middle of its fuzzy range.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What does “fail to reject the null” mean?

options.text: Evidence was insufficient under the test

rationales.whyCorrect: Hypothesis tests do not confirm exact equivalence by nonsignificance.
rationales.eli10: The jury lacked enough evidence; it did not prove nothing happened.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Power analysis before a study helps choose:

options.text: Sample size for a target effect

rationales.whyCorrect: It estimates observations needed for desired detection probability.
rationales.eli10: Plan how big a flashlight is needed to see the expected object.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A p value changes from 0.06 to 0.04 after adding data, but effect size is stable. What changed most?

rationales.whyCorrect: More data can reduce standard error without changing magnitude.
rationales.eli10: The same dot gained sharper edges and crossed the line.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Two studies estimate the same effect; one CI is narrower. It is:

rationales.whyCorrect: Interval width reflects sampling precision under assumptions.
rationales.eli10: Its fuzzy range is tighter.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why is p-hacking harmful?

options.text: Repeated analytic searching inflates false findings

rationales.whyCorrect: Unreported flexibility exploits random noise.
rationales.eli10: Trying many locks until one opens can mistake luck for a key.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A noninferiority trial requires special caution because:

options.text: A justified margin and design integrity are essential

rationales.whyCorrect: Poor conduct can falsely make treatments appear similar.
rationales.eli10: You must define how close is close and run a fair race.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which finding offers stronger evidence against the same null?

rationales.whyCorrect: Smaller p values are less compatible with the null model.
rationales.eli10: The clue is more surprising if nothing real is happening.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What should determine a research conclusion?

options.text: Effect, uncertainty, validity, and clinical context

rationales.whyCorrect: Responsible interpretation integrates magnitude, precision, design, and relevance.
rationales.eli10: Use every important clue, not one magic number.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Evidence-based practice integrates best evidence with:

rationales.whyCorrect: The approach combines research, professional judgment, and preferences.
rationales.eli10: Good care uses science, skill, and what matters to the person.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: An article abstract provides:

rationales.whyCorrect: Abstracts condense purpose, methods, results, and conclusions.
rationales.eli10: It is the article's short preview.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which section explains participant selection and procedures?

rationales.whyCorrect: Methods describe how the study was conducted.
rationales.eli10: This section tells the recipe used.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which section reports analyzed findings?

rationales.whyCorrect: The results section presents estimates, tables, and tests.
rationales.eli10: This is where the study shows what it found.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which section interprets findings and limitations?

rationales.whyCorrect: Discussion connects results to context and addresses weaknesses.
rationales.eli10: It explains what the findings may mean and where they wobble.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A systematic review uses:

options.text: Explicit methods to find and appraise studies

rationales.whyCorrect: Transparent searching and selection reduce cherry-picking.
rationales.eli10: It follows a careful map to collect all relevant puzzle pieces.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A meta-analysis statistically:

rationales.whyCorrect: It pools quantitative results when studies are sufficiently comparable.
rationales.eli10: It makes one larger estimate from several study answers.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which design best tests intervention efficacy?

rationales.whyCorrect: Randomized comparison reduces confounding.
rationales.eli10: Fairly shuffled teams give a strong treatment test.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Observational research is especially useful when:

options.text: Random assignment is unethical or impractical

rationales.whyCorrect: It can study real exposures that cannot responsibly be assigned.
rationales.eli10: Watch what happens when you cannot fairly choose the exposure.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why read beyond an abstract?

options.text: Important details and limitations may be omitted

rationales.whyCorrect: Brief summaries cannot fully show design quality or applicability.
rationales.eli10: A movie trailer does not reveal every plot problem.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A study's eligibility criteria help judge:

rationales.whyCorrect: Who was included determines whom results resemble.
rationales.eli10: Check whether the study crowd matches the people of interest.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why distinguish relative from absolute risk?

options.text: Relative effects can obscure baseline magnitude

rationales.whyCorrect: Both views are needed for understandable impact.
rationales.eli10: “Half as likely” means little until you know half of what.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A confidence interval around benefit is wide. This indicates:

rationales.whyCorrect: Many effect sizes remain compatible with the data.
rationales.eli10: The answer has broad fuzzy edges.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What does a study limitation section support?

rationales.whyCorrect: Limitations show where bias, uncertainty, or applicability may be restricted.
rationales.eli10: It marks cracks in the flashlight beam.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A systematic review finds highly inconsistent effects. What should readers examine?

options.text: Differences in populations, interventions, and methods

rationales.whyCorrect: Clinical and methodological heterogeneity may explain variation.
rationales.eli10: The puzzle pieces may come from different pictures.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why are randomized trials not always highest for every question?

options.text: Harms or long-term exposures may need observational evidence

rationales.whyCorrect: Design choice depends on question, feasibility, duration, and ethics.
rationales.eli10: Use the right tool for the job.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A surrogate outcome improves, but patient-important outcomes are unmeasured. Concern?

rationales.whyCorrect: Biomarker change may not translate into how people feel or function.
rationales.eli10: A dashboard light improved, but we do not know whether the ride did.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why disclose conflicts of interest?

options.text: To let readers assess potential influence

rationales.whyCorrect: Transparency supports critical appraisal of funding and incentives.
rationales.eli10: Readers should know who may have a reason to lean the story.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Replication by independent teams increases confidence because:

options.text: Findings recur under new investigators and samples

rationales.whyCorrect: Reproducibility reduces the chance a result was sample- or team-specific.
rationales.eli10: Different cooks following the recipe get a similar dish.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A guideline recommendation is strong despite low-certainty evidence. What should be checked?

rationales.whyCorrect: Recommendations integrate evidence certainty with consequences and preferences.
rationales.eli10: See why the panel chose firmly even with a dim flashlight.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which article feature best supports reproducibility?

rationales.whyCorrect: Detailed procedures allow others to repeat the work.
rationales.eli10: A complete recipe lets another cook try it.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A trial reports only relative reduction. What additional number is most useful?

rationales.whyCorrect: Absolute effects show expected event differences.
rationales.eli10: Tell how many people in each crowd had the event.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why should subgroup findings be prespecified?

options.text: Post hoc subgroup searching can create false patterns

rationales.whyCorrect: Advance plans reduce multiple-testing and data-mining concerns.
rationales.eli10: Choose the smaller teams before seeing which scoreboard looks exciting.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A meta-analysis pools biased small studies. Result may be:

rationales.whyCorrect: Pooling cannot erase systematic flaws in inputs.
rationales.eli10: Averaging crooked rulers gives a very sure wrong answer.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: How should evidence be applied when a person differs from study participants?

rationales.whyCorrect: Use evidence cautiously while considering relevant differences.
rationales.eli10: Ask whether the study shoes fit this person's feet.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A treatment's benefit is modest and harms uncertain. Best approach?

rationales.whyCorrect: Shared decisions should reflect tradeoffs and incomplete knowledge.
rationales.eli10: Lay out the knowns and unknowns before choosing.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why is publication bias a threat to reviews?

options.text: Positive studies may be easier to find

rationales.whyCorrect: Missing null studies can exaggerate pooled effects.
rationales.eli10: If only winning games are shown, the team looks too strong.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Two high-quality trials disagree. Best next step?

options.text: Examine chance, methods, populations, and interventions

rationales.whyCorrect: Differences or random variation may explain discordance.
rationales.eli10: Compare the recipes and diners before mixing the answers.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is responsible evidence use?

options.text: Match claims to design, precision, and applicability

rationales.whyCorrect: Conclusions should not exceed what methods and data support.
rationales.eli10: Keep the answer inside the flashlight's beam.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A clinically important effect has a CI spanning benefit and harm. Conclusion?

options.text: More evidence is needed because uncertainty crosses both

rationales.whyCorrect: The interval cannot exclude meaningfully opposite outcomes.
rationales.eli10: The fuzzy range covers both helping and hurting.
